item.research_question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the maximum strength and dislocation patterning in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs)?
item.processing_route: Hybrid Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation
item.test_conditions: Uniaxial tensile deformation at a constant engineering strain rate of 10^8 s^-1 and temperature of 300 K
key_findings: The presence of SRO appreciably increases the maximum strength and lowers the propensity for faulting and structure transformation
SRO increases the stacking fault energy (SFE) and activation energy barrier of dislocation motion
Grain orientation plays a crucial role in deformation mechanisms, microstructure evolution, and dislocation patterning
The volume fraction of deformation-induced hcp atoms is decreased in SRO systems compared to random solid solution (RSS) systems
SRO systems exhibit extended and strain-concentrated planar slip nanobands, implying repetitive dislocation glide
item.mechanism: The interplay between SRO, SFE, and antiphase boundary generation exerts back stress on moving dislocations, retarding their motion and enhancing solid solution strengthening
item.limitations: The imposed straining rate in the simulations is several orders of magnitude higher than that of conventional laboratory experiments
item.future_work: Further study on the effects of SRO on grain boundary sliding and migration, and the exploration of tunable chemical order at short-range or even medium-range distances
quotes: The presence of SRO appreciably increases the maximum strength and lowers the propensity for faulting and structure transformation

The interplay between SF creation, antiphase boundary generation, and the associated energy penalty, stemming from the existence of SRO, exerts back stress on moving dislocation and retards its motion

records.text: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the maximum strength and dislocation patterning in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs)?. System: CrCoNi-based alloys. Processing: Hybrid Monte Carlo (MC) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile deformation at a constant engineering strain rate of 10^8 s^-1 and temperature of 300 K. Findings: The presence of SRO appreciably increases the maximum strength and lowers the propensity for faulting and structure transformation; SRO increases the stacking fault energy (SFE) and activation energy barrier of dislocation motion; Grain orientation plays a crucial role in deformation mechanisms, microstructure evolution, and dislocation patterning; The volume fraction of deformation-induced hcp atoms is decreased in SRO systems compared to random solid solution (RSS) systems; SRO systems exhibit extended and strain-concentrated planar slip nanobands, implying repetitive dislocation glide. Mechanism: The interplay between SRO, SFE, and antiphase boundary generation exerts back stress on moving dislocations, retarding their motion and enhancing solid solution strengthening. Limitations: The imposed straining rate in the simulations is several orders of magnitude higher than that of conventional laboratory experiments. Future work: Further study on the effects of SRO on grain boundary sliding and migration, and the exploration of tunable chemical order at short-range or even medium-range distances. Quote: "The presence of SRO appreciably increases the maximum strength and lowers the propensity for faulting and structure transformation"
